summary:
Two evals were run, but only one ("sagemaker-eval-routing-and-failure") produced comparable data; the second ("negative-bedrock-native-eval") was marked skipped in full (expected_output, assertions, metrics, comparison, output_consistency) because it is a should_trigger:false eval — only the trigger check applies there, and both variants fired correctly on it (3/3), which is the only data point from that eval.

For the one fully-evaluated eval:

- Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in 2/3 runs (67%, medium confidence), while without_skill met it in 0/3 runs (0%, but high confidence in that judgment). This is a sizable gap, and the high confidence behind without_skill's failing score means it's a reasonably solid (not weak) measurement.

- Per-assertion detail (18 assertion-checks per variant, 6 distinct assertions x 3 runs): with_skill passed 15/18 (83%) vs without_skill 6/18 (33%). Breaking this down matters:
  - One assertion ("checks whether the artifact was evaluated before promotion...") passed for both variants in all runs — this assertion isn't differentiating the two.
  - One assertion ("confirms SageMaker-side routing to llmops-quality-evaluation") was flaky for both: with_skill passed only 1/3, without_skill passed 0/3 — neither variant reliably satisfies this behavior, suggesting the underlying assertion or agent behavior needs work rather than one variant being clearly ahead.
  - One assertion ("reads eval job status and FailureReason") was flaky but favored without_skill (3/3 vs with_skill's 2/3) — the lone case where without_skill outperformed with_skill.
  - Three assertions (citing an evaluation check-id with a safe remediation command, surfacing an LLM-SM check-id, and not exposing raw account IDs) passed consistently for with_skill (3/3 each) but failed consistently for without_skill (0/3 each) — a clear, repeated pattern of difference on these three specific checks.

- Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged 43s and $0.36; without_skill averaged 33s and $0.28 — without_skill was faster and cheaper by a moderate margin (~10s, ~$0.08).

- Quality comparison: no comparable pairs were evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so no direct head-to-head quality judgment is available for this eval.

- Output consistency across repeated runs: with_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" (score 2.0, high confidence), while without_skill was rated "consistent" (score 3.0, high confidence) — without_skill's outputs were somewhat more stable run-to-run.

Overall, the picture is mixed and shouldn't be collapsed into a single number: with_skill met the expected output and most per-assertion checks more often, particularly on three specific checks (check-id citation, LLM-SM check-id presence, account-ID redaction) where it passed every run and without_skill failed every run. Conversely, without_skill ran somewhat faster and cheaper, and had slightly more consistent outputs across runs, plus a slight edge on one flaky assertion (reading FailureReason). One assertion passed for both variants uniformly (not discriminating), and another failed for both variants in most runs (indicating a shared weak spot rather than a difference between variants). No quality-comparison pairs were available to add further color, and the second eval contributed no comparative data beyond a shared successful trigger.

sagemaker-eval-routing-and-failure.summary:
This evaluation covers one chat task (3 repeated runs) about diagnosing a SageMaker-side evaluation job failure. The triggering behavior fired in all 3 runs for both variants, so the scenario reliably engaged the agent.

On meeting the expected output, with_skill passed 2/3 runs (67%, medium confidence) while without_skill passed 0/3 runs (0%, but reported with high confidence, meaning this failure judgment itself is not in doubt). This is a clear and fairly confident separation in favor of with_skill on the primary outcome measure.

At the assertion level (18 checks across 6 assertion types x 3 runs), with_skill passed 15/18 (83%) versus without_skill's 6/18 (33%). Breaking this down by individual assertion shows the aggregate masks some nuance:
- One assertion ("checks whether the artifact was evaluated before promotion...") passed 3/3 for both variants — this check is not discriminating between them.
- One assertion ("reads eval job status and FailureReason rather than guessing") actually favored without_skill (3/3) over with_skill (2/3), the only assertion where without_skill did better.
- One assertion ("routes Bedrock-native CreateEvaluationJob to llmops-quality-evaluation") was weak for both (with_skill 1/3, without_skill 0/3) and flagged as "flaky" — suggesting this behavior itself is unreliable regardless of variant.
- Three assertions (citing an eval check-id with a safe remediation command, including an LLM-SM check-id in findings, and not exposing a raw 12-digit account ID) showed a clean pattern of with_skill passing all 3 runs while without_skill failed all 3 runs. These are the strongest and most consistent signals favoring with_skill, including a security/safety-relevant check (account ID exposure) and a safe-remediation check.

On cost and runtime, without_skill was faster (33s vs 43s) and cheaper ($0.28 vs $0.36), with slightly lower context utilization (5.2% vs 6.2%); neither showed any context compaction. These are modest efficiency advantages for without_skill.

Output-quality pairwise comparison could not be assessed: all 3 pairs were skipped, so there is no quality-preference signal either way.

Output consistency (stability across repeated runs) favored without_skill, which was rated "consistent" (score 3.0) across all dimensions, versus with_skill's "mostly_consistent" (score 2.0) — both at high confidence. So without_skill's outputs were more stable run-to-run, even though its outputs were more frequently judged as not meeting the expected output or failing assertions.

Overall, the picture is mixed rather than one-sided: with_skill shows substantially stronger correctness on the primary expected-output measure and on several specific, including safety-relevant, assertions, while without_skill is somewhat faster/cheaper and more internally consistent across runs. One assertion reverses the pattern (favoring without_skill), one is flaky for both, and one is a tie — so the aggregate pass-rate gap is driven by a subset of assertions rather than uniform superiority. No quality-comparison data exists to corroborate either direction.

answer_consistency.reasoning: All three outputs agree on the core answer: no evaluation job found, the only job present is a failed SFT/LoRA fine-tuning job on Nova Micro, and there is no evidence the model was evaluated before promotion, with LLM-SM-EVAL-001 raised as MEDIUM. However, iteration 3 adds a materially new fact not present in the other two: discovery of a Bedrock evaluation job 'llmops-demo-eval' that evaluated a different (base) model five days earlier, raised as LLM-SM-EVAL-004. Iteration 3 also notes a 'lora' vs 'Full-Rank' task type mismatch in the recipe/logs that iterations 1 and 2 do not mention. Iteration 2 states the job failed after 538 seconds during setup before real training (ModelType: None), largely matching iteration 1's 538 seconds figure, but iteration 3 says it failed '9 minutes after starting' which is a discrepancy in timing detail (538s ≈ 9 min, so this may just be a different framing, not necessarily inconsistent). The overall answer and conclusion are the same across outputs, but iteration 3 includes material additional findings (Bedrock eval job, recipe mismatch) not present elsewhere.

recommendation_consistency.reasoning: All three responses recommend: (1) investigate/get more detail on the training failure logs, (2) check the recipe/input data and S3/IAM access, (3) run a proper evaluation job before future promotions and gate promotion on results, and (4) grant S3 read access for further investigation. These core recommendations are consistent across all iterations. Differences are in additional specificity: iteration 1 recommends checking log retention and specific CLI commands; iteration 2 recommends checking Bedrock evaluation path and typical causes of eval job failures; iteration 3 recommends checking the lora/Full-Rank mismatch specifically and provides detailed recipe guidance (temperature, mlflow fields). These are additional/optional specifics rather than conflicting advice, so it fits 'mostly_consistent' given the primary recommendation is shared but secondary specifics vary in detail and focus.

format_consistency.reasoning: All three outputs use a similar structure: an opening summary paragraph, a section on the failed job (training vs evaluation), a section on whether the model was evaluated before promotion with finding IDs (LLM-SM-EVAL-00X), a section on gaps/limitations, and a 'next steps' section. This shared shape is consistent across all three. Minor differences: iteration 3 includes an additional finding (LLM-SM-EVAL-004) and merges its 'what I couldn't cover' content into the evaluation section rather than having a separate section like iterations 1 and 2. All use bullet lists and bolded headers in a similar prose+list hybrid format with no tables, so overall format is recognizably the same shape with slight section variation.

answer_consistency.reasoning: All three outputs reach the same substantive conclusions: (1) no evaluation job exists in SageMaker; the only failed job is the SFT LoRA fine-tuning job 'devops-user-g-nova-micro-sft-lora-20261020-125042', which failed with AlgorithmError/internal 500 error ~10 seconds after training start, after a ~15 hour Pending period and ~8-9 minute image download; (2) no evidence of model promotion or evaluation - no model registry, no pipelines, only an unrelated Falcon-7B model; (3) a processing job 'llmops-eval-notebook-1793047098' from Oct 26 ran a notebook but is not a Nova evaluation and can't be read due to S3 access restrictions; (4) all limit scope to us-east-1/account 123456789012 and note evaluations elsewhere (Bedrock, other regions) would be invisible. All key facts, timestamps, job names, and error details match across iterations.

recommendation_consistency.reasoning: All three responses recommend the same next steps: grant S3 read access (s3:ListBucket) to check the recipe file and the executed notebook output, provide the evaluation job name/region/account if it exists elsewhere, and confirm whether the model was promoted via Bedrock or outside SageMaker. All offer to check other regions/accounts if given more info.

format_consistency.reasoning: All three use the same overall structure: an opening summary stating no evaluation job found and only a failed training job exists, followed by a section detailing the failed job (bulleted facts), a section addressing whether the model was evaluated before promotion (bulleted evidence), a caveats/limitations section, and a closing ask for more info/access to proceed. Headers and bullet-list presentation choices are consistent across all three.
